Demon Possession
DEE-muhn puh-ZESH-uhn
noun (spiritual bondage)
From Greek daimonizomai, to be demonized or possessed by a demon; possession from Latin possidere, to hold or occupy, here the seizing of a person by an evil spirit.

📖 Biblical Definition

Demon possession is the real and dreadful bondage of a person to one or more evil spirits, who indwell, torment, and at times control the one possessed, until Christ or His authority drives them out. The Greek daimonizomai, rendered "possessed with devils," describes a true seizure of body and faculties, not mere illness or superstition. The Gospels record many such cases: the Gadarene held by a legion of unclean spirits (Mark 5), the two fierce men of the tombs whom none could pass by (Matt 8:28), and the damsel with a spirit of divination whom Paul delivered (Acts 16:16-18). In every case the demons are real persons, malignant and intelligent, subject wholly to the word of Christ, who casts them out with authority and power. Yet Scripture sets sober bounds: the apostolic age of attesting signs has closed, and the believer is not to chase sensational deliverances nor to credit every affliction to a demon. The cessationist temper holds both truths, the reality of the demonic and the sufficiency of Christ's finished triumph over the powers (Col 2:15). This dictionary confesses that evil spirits are real and dangerous, that Christ reigns sovereign over them all, and that the saint resists the devil by faith, the word, and prayer, not by spectacle.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Demon possession is the real bondage of a person to evil spirits who indwell and torment until Christ casts them out. The Gospels record true seizures, not mere illness, all subject to Christ's sovereign authority. A cessationist sobriety holds the demonic to be real while rejecting sensationalism.

DEMON POSSESSION, noun. The real seizure and bondage of a person by one or more evil spirits.

It renders the Greek daimonizomai, to be demonized, describing a true indwelling, not mere disease or superstition.

"And they that were possessed with devils came to him; and he cast out the spirits with his word" (cf. Matt 8:16).

It requires sober vigilance and reliance on Christ's authority; it forbids both denial of the demonic and sensational hunting after it.

It stands wholly under the dominion of Christ, who spoiled principalities and powers and triumphed over them openly.

📖 Key Scripture

Mark 5:8 — "For he said unto him, Come out of the man, thou unclean spirit."

Matt 8:28 — "And when he was come to the other side into the country of the Gergesenes, there met him two possessed with devils, coming out of the tombs, exceeding fierce, so that no man might pass by that way."

Acts 16:18 — "And this did she many days. But Paul, being grieved, turned and said to the spirit, I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And he came out the same hour."

Col 2:15 — "And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Two errors flank the truth: a rationalism that explains the demonic away as mere illness or myth, and a sensationalism that sees demons behind every affliction and trades on spectacle.

expand to see more

Liberal and naturalistic readers dismiss the Gospel accounts as primitive misunderstandings of epilepsy or madness, denying the reality of evil spirits that Christ Himself addressed as persons. On the opposite hand, much charismatic and continuationist practice runs to the other extreme, attributing every sin, sickness, and sorrow to a demon and staging dramatic deliverances as a kind of theater. Both dishonor the plain teaching of Scripture, the one by unbelief, the other by excess.

Recover the cessationist sobriety that takes the demonic seriously yet soberly. Evil spirits are real, malignant, and intelligent, but they are wholly subject to Christ, who spoiled the principalities and powers at the cross. The believer is not left to spectacle but is armed with the whole armor of God, resisting the devil by faith, the word, and prayer, assured that greater is He that is in us than he that is in the world.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word renders Greek daimonizomai, to be demonized, the seizing of a person by an unclean spirit.

expand to see more

Greek daimonizomai, to be demonized, is the verb the Gospels use for those possessed with devils.

Greek daimonion, demon, names the evil spirit itself, a fallen and malignant person.

The phrase pneuma akatharton, unclean spirit, is used interchangeably in Mark 5.

Latin possidere, to hold or occupy, gives the English possession, the spirit's seizing of its victim.

Col 2:15 shows the demonic powers spoiled and openly triumphed over by Christ at the cross.

Usage

"He affirmed the reality of demon possession in the Gospels without crediting every illness to a demon."

"The unclean spirits obeyed Christ's word at once, proof of His sovereign authority over the demonic."

"Cessationist sobriety guards the church from both denying the demonic and chasing sensational deliverances."
